title: Sleep in the rule
hookLine: write your sleep hours into your rule: Jesus slept in the stern through a storm, and a psalm calls sleep a gift
tomorrow: a cook's knife stayed sharp for nineteen years. what was his secret?

lines: A WHOLE DAY TEACHING FROM A BOAT.
cards: Late nights have a way of making the to-do list look endless. Jesus had a long day once, by the sea. The crowd was so large that he got into a boat and sat in it on the sea, teaching the people on the shore until evening.
Then he said to his friends: "Let us pass over unto the other side." Out on the water a great storm of wind came up. The waves beat into the ship until it was filling.
And where was Jesus? Mark says: "he was in the hinder part of the ship, asleep on a pillow."

teach.b: They woke him: "Master, carest thou not that we perish?"
He got up, rebuked the wind, and said to the sea, "Peace, be still." The wind dropped, and there was a great calm. Then he turned to them with his own question: why are ye so fearful?
Look at the order Mark keeps. A full day of giving. Then sleep, with the boat pitching under him.
Then the calm. In this Gospel, the one who could quiet the storm was also the one who could sleep in it. Here's the teaching under the story.
In these texts, sleep isn't laziness and it isn't lost time. It's a gift, and lying down is an act of trust.
A psalm says it outright: it's vain to rise up early and sit up late, "for so he giveth his beloved sleep."
Another psalm is headed as David's, from the time he fled from his own son Absalom, with enemies rising against him.

teach.h: I LAID ME DOWN AND SLEPT.
teach.b: Even there: "I laid me down and slept; I awaked; for the LORD sustained me." In these texts, sleep is received, not earned. Nobody gets it by finishing the list first.
For a rule of life, that means sleep goes in first, before the early alarms and the late screens, because every other line in the rule leans on it. The storm in the story still came.
The picture Mark leaves is a tired man in the stern, asleep anyway.

how: Monastic and personal rules of life can set fixed hours for sleep and rising. Christians read Jesus asleep in the storm, and Jews and Christians read Psalms 3 and 127, as reminders that sleep is a gift.

games.q: what does “sleep in the rule” mean?
o: a short nap taken in the middle of a long working day
cutting sleep short so there's more time for spiritual practice
writing your sleep hours into your rule before anything else

games.q: asleep in the storm: tap the pairs.
p: taught from a boat until evening

s: Jesus stayed awake on watch through the storm
Mark says he was asleep on a pillow in the stern until they woke him.
a psalm headed as David's, fleeing Absalom, says I laid me down and slept
Psalm 3:5: "I laid me down and slept; I awaked; for the LORD sustained me."
Psalm 127 praises rising early and sitting up late
it calls that vain: "for so he giveth his beloved sleep."

games.q: a friend is exhausted and asks for a spiritual book to fix it. by today's texts, what comes first?
o: sleep: Jesus slept after a full day, and the psalm calls sleep a gift.
the book: real practice means staying up and pushing through the tiredness.
a long fast, to clear the mind before resting.
games.why: In these texts sleep comes first and is received as a gift: Jesus asleep in the stern, David lying down with enemies around him.

practice: Write your sleep hours into your rule: when you'll start winding down, when the lights go out, when you'll wake. Then put the pen down.
For the rest of the sit, let your shoulders drop and your breath slow, the way a body settles onto a pillow at the end of a long day.

wordCard.voice: Sleep in the rule: your sleep hours written into your rule of life, first, received as a gift, the way the psalm says he giveth his beloved sleep.

carryVoice: Your line: sleep first. Jesus slept in the stern after a full day, storm or no storm. Rest well, and it's day 1645.
